pedagogy.summary: By age 10-11 children must fuse three ideas they have met separately: that a fraction IS a division (a/b = a ÷ b), that dividing gives a decimal, and that fractions, decimals and percentages are three interchangeable names for one quantity. The pedagogical work is not teaching a new procedure but building fluent, flexible movement between the three forms so a child can pick whichever form makes a comparison easiest — e.g. converting 30%, 1/3 and 0.35 to a common form to order them. The load-bearing insight is that the fraction bar means 'divide the top by the bottom', which lets 3/8 be evaluated as 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
bestPractices: Establish the fraction-as-division meaning explicitly: 3/8 means 3 shared into 8, and 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 — connect the bar notation to a division the child can carry out.
Teach a small set of recall equivalents as landmarks (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 1/10, 1/3≈0.33) so children convert by memory for common cases and by division for the rest.
Make ordering across forms the core task: give mixed sets (30%, 1/3, 0.35) and require conversion to ONE common form before comparing — this is where the equivalence pays off.
Use the fact that percentages and decimals are hundredths and tenths to move fluidly (0.35 = 35% = 35/100), reserving division for fractions that aren't already tenths/hundredths.
Confront non-terminating cases honestly: 1/3 = 0.333... is NOT 0.3; round only when told to, and show why the division never stops.
keyRepresentations: Long/short division laid out for 3 ÷ 8 (with the decimal point and trailing zeros) to show a fraction becoming a decimal
A triple-labelled bar or hundred-grid showing the same shaded quantity named as fraction, decimal and percentage at once
A number line from 0 to 1 with fractions, decimals and percentages all plotted, so order is visible spatially
A double number line / equivalence table of the landmark fractions and their decimal & percentage partners
commonMisconceptions: Reverses the division: reads 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3 (divides the larger by the smaller out of habit), giving 2.67 instead of 0.375.
Compares mixed forms by surface digits — thinks 1/3 is largest of {30%, 1/3, 0.35} because '3 is a big number' or because the numbers look bigger, without converting to a common form.
Treats 1/3 as exactly 0.3 (or 0.33) and terminating, not recognising the recurring decimal.
Believes every fraction gives a neat terminating decimal, so is thrown when a division doesn't stop.

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, the goal is fluent, flexible movement between fractions, decimals and percentages as three names for one quantity. The load-bearing insight is that the fraction bar means 'divide the top by the bottom', so 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Learners should pick whichever form makes a comparison easiest, converting a mixed set to one common form before ordering (e.g. 30%, 1/3, 0.35 → 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35, so the order is 30% < 1/3 < 0.35). Note that 1/3 landing between 30% and 0.35 is counter-intuitive and is where the surface-digit misconception is confronted.

activities.title: Watch a fraction become a decimal: 3 ÷ 8
feedback: If you got 2.67, you divided 8 by 3 instead of 3 by 8. Re-read 3/8 as '3 shared among 8', which must be less than one whole — so it is 3 ÷ 8.
Model it concretely: 3 pizzas shared among 8 people gives each person less than half a pizza, so the answer must be below 1.
If you wrote 1/3 = 0.3, keep dividing 1 ÷ 3: the 3s never stop, so 1/3 is a little bigger than 0.3 and bigger than 30%.
If a division doesn't stop, that's expected for fractions like 1/3 — not every fraction gives a neat terminating decimal.
activities.rationale: Connecting bar notation to a division the learner actually carries out builds the fraction-as-division meaning, and watching a recurring case confronts the belief that every fraction terminates. Predicting before dividing surfaces the reversed-division habit at a teachable moment.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [for example, 0.375] for a simple fraction [for example, 3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents pupils learn about rounding to three decimal places (statutory wording + notes).
Fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence and ordering across forms is a key Year 6 structural connection; the fraction bar (vinculum) is understood as a division.

Children commonly reverse fraction-as-division, computing a/b as b/a (dividing the larger by the smaller), rooted in the primitive 'divisor must be smaller than dividend / division makes smaller' model.
learnerActions: Before dividing, predict: will 3/8 be more than 1 or less than 1, and roughly what? Say why (3 shared among 8 people is less than one whole).
Carry out the division 3.000 ÷ 8 step by step, keeping the decimal point and trailing zeros, to reach 0.375.
Compare the result against your prediction. If you predicted more than 1, check whether you divided 3 by 8 or 8 by 3.
Try a case that never stops: carry out 1 ÷ 3 far enough to see 0.333... keep repeating, and note it does NOT equal 0.3.
Round only when told to (e.g. 1/3 ≈ 0.333 to three decimal places), and explain why the division never terminates.
activities.intendedInsight: The fraction bar means 'divide the numerator by the denominator'; 3/8 is 3 ÷ 8, and some divisions (like 1 ÷ 3) produce recurring, non-terminating decimals.

activities.title: Order a mixed set by converting to a common form
feedback: If you ranked 1/3 largest 'because 3 is a big number', convert first: 1/3 = 0.333..., which lands between 0.30 and 0.35.
Comparing by how big the written digits look is unreliable; the number line places each value by its converted size, so the order falls out of position.
To turn 30% into a comparable form, use that per cent means 'out of 100': 30% = 0.30 = 30/100.
If you treated 1/3 as exactly 0.3, place 1/3 and 0.3 as separate points — 1/3 is slightly to the right (0.333... > 0.30), so 1/3 > 30%.
activities.rationale: Ordering across forms is where cross-form equivalence pays off; requiring conversion to a common form before comparing directly targets the documented surface-digit error, and the counter-intuitive placement of 1/3 makes the need to convert felt.
sourceClaims: Comparing and ordering fractions, decimals and percentages requires converting to a common representation; comparing by surface digits (which look bigger) is a persistent, documented error.
Fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence and ordering across forms is a key Year 6 structural connection; the fraction bar (vinculum) is understood as a division.
learnerActions: Take the set 30%, 1/3 and 0.35. First predict the order smallest→largest by eye, and say why.
Convert all three to ONE common form (decimals: 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35), using that percentages are hundredths and division for 1/3.
Plot each converted value on a 0-1 number line and read off the order from position, not appearance.
Compare your conversion-based order (30% < 1/3 < 0.35) with your by-eye prediction and note where they differed — especially whether you expected 1/3 to be biggest.
Transfer the method to a new set, e.g. 30%, 2/5, 0.35: convert each (0.30, 0.40, 0.35) and say where 2/5 goes, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Different forms cannot be reliably compared by surface digits; converting every item to one common form (then plotting on a line) makes the true order visible — and 1/3 sits between 30% and 0.35.

activities.title: Build a landmark equivalence set
feedback: If you wrote 1/3 = 0.33 exactly, flag it as approximate: the decimal recurs (0.333...), so 1/3 is a touch above 0.33 and above 30%.
Use the hundredths/tenths link to move fluidly: 0.35 = 35% = 35/100 without any new division.
A triple-labelled bar is for consolidating recall; pair it with the division and ordering tasks to practise flexible conversion, not just memory.
activities.rationale: A small set of recalled equivalents reduces load for common conversions so effort can go to the ordering work, and a shared representation reinforces that one quantity has three interchangeable names; noting which landmarks recur keeps rounding honest.
sourceClaims: Fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence and ordering across forms is a key Year 6 structural connection; the fraction bar (vinculum) is understood as a division.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [for example, 0.375] for a simple fraction [for example, 3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents pupils learn about rounding to three decimal places (statutory wording + notes).
learnerActions: For each landmark, show all three names on one shared bar or hundred-grid so the same shaded quantity is seen as fraction, decimal and percentage at once.

Match a form to its partners from memory (e.g. given 1/5, recall 0.2 and 20%); for fractions that are not landmarks, rewrite them as tenths or hundredths where easy (e.g. 3/20 = 15/100), and otherwise use division.
Note which landmarks are exact and which (like 1/3) are recurring, so you don't record 1/3 as a terminating 0.33.
activities.intendedInsight: Memorised landmark equivalents let you convert common cases instantly, reserving division for less familiar fractions, while a shared visual shows the three forms name one quantity.

constraints: A tap-to-reveal triple-labelled bar of landmark equivalents consolidates recall but does not let the learner choose and carry out a division or order an arbitrary mixed set, so it builds memory rather than the flexible conversion at the heart of this topic — pair it with active division and ordering work.

Recognition and matching checks (e.g. pairing 1/5↔0.2↔20%, or ordering a given set) can confirm the target skill but do not by themselves require the learner to independently construct a conversion; include tasks where the learner carries out 3 ÷ 8 and explains their ordering.
1/3 does not equal 0.3 or exactly 0.33: it is the recurring 0.333..., so it is slightly larger than 30%. Round only when instructed, and treat 33.3% as a rounded value too.
Read 3/8 as 3 ÷ 8 (numerator ÷ denominator), not 8 ÷ 3; the reversed division giving 2.67 is a misconception to correct, never a valid answer.

Interactive panels (a digit-by-digit division display, a draggable 0-1 ordering line, a convert-to-common-form toggle) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not required equipment, and the same tasks can be done on paper.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 (confirmed). The reversed 8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.666... ≈ 2.67 (confirmed as the misconception distractor, kept only in feedback/diagnosis, never as a valid answer). 1 ÷ 3 = 0.333... recurring (confirmed). Order 0.30 < 0.333... < 0.35, i.e. 30% < 1/3 < 0.35 (confirmed). Transfer set 2/5 = 0.40, so 30% < 0.35 < 2/5 (confirmed).

The source claim about reversing fraction-as-division (Fischbein et al.; Tirosh & Graeber) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat the cited mechanism as informative background, not established fact, in activity 1.
The original stated 1/3 ≈ 0.33 as a landmark; retained but flagged as approximate/recurring (0.333... ≈ 33.3%) to avoid teaching it as terminating or as an exact percentage.

Activity 3's sourceClaims: the NCETM structural-connection claim is the direct support for the three-interchangeable-names/recall principle; the statutory claim is retained only because action 4 covers the recurring/rounding sub-action, and gives partial (sub-action) support, not full principle support. No new source verification was performed.

assess.poeTask: Before dividing: 'I'm going to work out 3/8 as a decimal. First predict — will it be more than 1 or less than 1, and roughly what? Say why.' A child holding fraction-as-division predicts less than 1 (3 shared among 8) near a third-ish; a child reversing the division predicts more than 1 (8÷3). Then carry out 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 and compare against the prediction — the mismatch is the teachable moment for the reversed-division child.
probeDeeper: You said 3/8 = 0.375 — is that bigger or smaller than 1? How do you know from the fraction itself?
How did you turn 30% into something you could compare with 1/3?
What if I'd asked you to order 30%, 2/5 and 0.35 instead — where would 2/5 go, and why?
Someone says 1/3 must be the biggest because 3 is the biggest number in the list. What would you say to them?
assess.correctAnswer: 3/8 = 0.375, found by dividing 3 ÷ 8. Order: 30% < 1/3 < 0.35 (i.e. 0.30 < 0.333... < 0.35), compared by converting all three to the same form — decimals: 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the fraction-as-division: 'I divide the big number by the small one, so 3/8 is 8 ÷ 3 = 2.67' — divides larger by smaller out of whole-number habit.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the meaning of the bar: 3/8 is 3 things shared among 8, which must be less than one, so it is 3 ÷ 8. Model with 3 pizzas shared by 8 people before re-doing the division.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 3/8 = 2.6 or 2.67, or says 'it's more than 1', and the shown method divides 8 by 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares mixed forms by surface digits: 'the biggest is 1/3 because 3, and 0.35 is smallest because it's tiny decimals' — ranks by how big the visible digits look rather than converting to a common form.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on converting all three to one form first; use a 0-1 number line and plot each after converting, so the child sees the ordering fall out of position, not appearance.
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/3 < 0.35 < 30% (ordered by how small the written numbers look)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders without converting, e.g. places 1/3 largest or 0.35 smallest; explanation cites the size of the digits, not a common form.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 1/3 as exactly 0.3 and terminating: 'one third is 0.3, so it's less than 0.35 and equal to 30%' — collapses the recurring decimal to one tenth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Carry out 1 ÷ 3 far enough to see 0.333... never stop; place 1/3 and 0.3 as distinct points on the line and show 1/3 is a little bigger than 0.3, hence bigger than 30%.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 1/3 = 0.3 and consequently rates 1/3 = 30%, or cannot decide between 1/3 and 30%.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot convert 3/8 (or reverses to 8÷3), and orders the mixed set by appearance of digits with no conversion; cannot say how the three forms relate.
responseLevels.full: Divides 3÷8 = 0.375 the right way round, converts all of 30%, 1/3, 0.35 to a common form, orders them 30% < 1/3 < 0.35, and explains that comparison requires a shared form — transferring the method to a new item (e.g. 2/5) without prompting.
responseLevels.partial: Converts 3/8 correctly and knows the landmark equivalents, and can name each form, but when ordering the mixed set either doesn't convert to a common form or converts only some, so the ordering is unreliable and the comparison isn't explained.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Convert 3/8 to a decimal and show how you got it. Then take 30%, 1/3 and 0.35, put them in order from smallest to largest, and tell me how you compared them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who genuinely holds fraction-as-division and cross-form equivalence divides 3÷8 the right way round AND converts the mixed set to a common form before ordering. A child operating on surface features reveals it two ways that a correct reasoner never would: dividing 8÷3 (bigger-by-smaller habit) and ranking 1/3 as largest 'because 3'. The reason-tier ('how you compared them') is what separates a lucky ordering from real equivalence reasoning — 1/3 sitting between 30% and 0.35 is counter-intuitive, so getting it right for a stated reason is hard to fake.
